TITLE 13 Preface 

A significant forward step in the legislation of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico was made with the passage of the Rules and Regulations Act of 1958, Act June 30, 1957, No. 112, 3

L.P.R.A. §§ 1041 to 1059. 

Laws of Puerto Rico Annotated made available to the citizens of the Commonwealth the laws enacted by the Legislative Branch and the interpretation of those laws by the Judicial Branch. The Rules and Regulations Act performs the same service with respect to the regulations adopted by the Executive Branch for the execution of the laws. 

The regulatory system set up by this Act has two principal features: (1) All regulations which are within the scope of the Act must be filed in the office of the Secretary of State. Beginning three months after June 30, 1957, any such regulation which is not filed with the Secretary of State is void and ineffective. 

This provides an official record of the regulations. (2) For the information and guidance of the people, these regulations will be published by the Secretary of State. This publication will be in two stages: (a) The "Rules and Regulations of Puerto Rico", for which the citation "R.&R.P.R." has been adopted, will be a codification of all regulations originally filed. (b) The "Puerto Rico Register" will be published periodically and will contain new regulations and amendments to existing regulations, thus keeping R.&R.P.R. up to date. After publication of the Register begins, new regulations will not become effective until published therein, except in cases of emergency. 

Rules and Regulations of Puerto Rico. The regulations originally filed with the Secretary of State have been classified by subject matter. A system of arrangement and numbering has been adopted which greatly simplifies the search for the corresponding provisions of the laws and regulations. For this purpose, R.&R.P.R. will have the same title and chapter numbers as Laws of Puerto Rico Annotated (L.P.R.A.). Regulations interpreting and applying a law contained in a title and chapter of L.P.R.A. will be found in the same title and chapter of R.&R.P.R. In addition, the 

VII

section numbers of a regulation in R.&R.P.R. will correspond with the section number of L.P.R.A. which authorizes the adoption of that regulation. For example, regulations adopted under 

With this system a person reading a provision of the law can find the corresponding regulations and a person reading the regulations can find the corresponding law without an extensive search of indexes and tables. 

Editorial features. The regulations have been arranged by titles. 

The text has been carefully edited and appropriate catchlines have been supplied. A source note under the first section of each regulation shows the agency which issued it, the approval date, the effective date if one is specified, the date of filing with the Secretary of State, and the File Number which it bears in the records of his office. The statutory authority for the adoption of the regulation is cited. Annotations of court decisions interpreting the regulations have been inserted. 

This set of R.&R.P.R. is published in both Spanish and English editions. Except in a few cases where the contrary clearly appears, the Spanish text has been treated as the official version. 

In some instances it has been necessary to change the English text as filed with the Secretary of State in order to correct apparent errors of translation.

Index and Tables. This volume contains a topical index of the titles which it covers. When the entire set is finished, the last volume will contain a complete and detailed index of all the titles. 

The Table of Agencies at the end of this volume, showing the regulations adopted by each agency which are included in these titles, will be replaced by a complete table at the end of the set showing all regulations of all agencies. 

Supplementation; Puerto Rico Register. R.&R.P.R. will be kept up to date by means of the Puerto Rico Register, which will be published periodically. This will be in the form of loose leaf pages, containing all changes and new provisions, which will be inserted in the original volumes of R.&R.P.R., replacing pages which have become obsolete. Thus, R.&R.P.R. will always be up to date with the latest issue of the Puerto Rico Register.

Printing and Binding. This volume has been produced in loose leaf form so that changes and new regulations can be incor- (5 

VIII

porated into R.&R.P.R. as quickly as possible after they become effective, and each section of the work will always be up to the minute.

This loose leaf ring binder has been chosen after exhaustive study of all available types of binders. Among its practical advantages are: (1) The pages lie absolutely flat no matter where you open it; (2) there are no hidden inner margins to force you to pry the pages apart in order to read them; and (3) pages can be inserted and removed with minimum time and effort. To insure durability under constant use, we have employed a quality paper throughout and strengthened the title tabs with cloth-reinforced holes.

In Appreciation. We acknowledge gratefully the advice, help, and constructive cooperation of all who made this set possible. 

Special appreciation is due the Secretary of State, Honorable 

Roberto Sanchez-Vilella, and Assistant Secretary of State, Honorable Nicolas Almiroty, for their effective cooperation and wise counsel in the planning and execution of this project, and to Honorable Hiram Torres Rigual, Executive Assistant to the Governor, whose vision and tireless efforts assured the success of this undertaking.

As in Laws of Puerto Rico Annotated, the Spanish edition of this set was edited by Mr. Ignacio Rivera, Secretary of the 

Supreme Court of Puerto Rico. His great ability, wise judgment, and devotion to a high ideal deserve full credit for the excellence of this edition.

Conclusion. Equity Publishing Corporation, which performed the editorial work on Laws of Puerto Rico Annotated, is especially proud to have been chosen to edit and publish these Rules and Regulations of Puerto Rico, under a contract with the Secretary of State. We consider it a privilege to have this part in the progress and accomplishments of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico.

§ 3181-1. Distributions by partnerships taxable to partners 

Partnerships as such are subject to the income tax imposed by chapter 252 of L.P.R.A., Title 13. For definition of what the term 

"partnership" includes, see sec. 3411(a) (3). Section 3181 requires that persons carrying on business in partnership shall include in their gross income for the taxable year the amount of their respective shares of the partnership profits distributed. See sec. 3182 for the meaning of the term "partnership profits distributed". § 3182. Definition of partnership profits distributed 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3182.] 

§ 3182-1. Partnership profits distributed (a) The term "partnership profits distributed" comprises any distribution in the ordinary course of business, even though extraordinary in amount, made by a partnership to its partners or participants, whether in money or other property (1) out of its earnings or profits accumulated after February 28, 1913, or (2) out of the earnings or profits of the taxable year (computed as of the close of the taxable year without diminution by reason of any distributions made during the taxable year), without regard to

Ch. 253 the amount of the earnings and profits at the time the distribution was made, except that— (i) Earnings and profits accumulated during taxable years beginning after December 31, 1939, and ending prior to January 1, 1951 (for which taxable years earnings and profits were taxable to the partners or participants whether distributed or not, by Act 

No. 31, approved April 12, 1941 [13 L.P.R.A. §§ 735, 737, 738, and 

744 to 747]), shall be excluded. (b) In determining whether a distribution is out of earnings or profits accumulated during taxable years beginning after December 31, 1939, and ending prior to January 1, 1951, due consideration must be given to the facts, and mere bookkeeping entries increasing or decreasing surplus will not be conclusive. (c) In the case of a partnership where depreciation is a factor in determining income, the only depreciation adjustment to be considered in the computation of earnings and profits available for distribution shall be made only with reference to the current depreciation provided in sec. 3023 (1) and without considering any option for or deduction of flexible depreciation under sec. 3114A.

1967 amendment note under § 3023(i)(1) of this title. 

ANNOTATIONS 

1. Prior regulation—Generally. From and after the amendment of the Income Tax Act by Act No. 31 of 1941, partnership profits were taxable to the partners even if they were not distributed in the taxable year in which they were realized. 

The tax thus imposed upon the persons with the right to share in such undistributed earnings was not intended for those persons having the right to share in the earnings or profits of the entities and organizations mentioned in 

§ 2(a)(2) of the Income Tax Act [13 L.P.R.A. § 632(a)(2)], or included in the general meaning of associations, according to that same section. Descartes, Treasurer v. Tax Court; 

Dávila, Int., 1957, 79 P.R.R. 818. 

§ 3183. Source of distributions [Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3183.] § 3183-1. Source of distributions 

For the purpose of income taxation every distribution made by a partnership is made out of earnings or profits to the extent thereof, and the most recently accumulated earnings or profits. 

Feb. 29, 1968 

Vol. 7, No. 2

Supp. F

T.13 § 3185-1 

PARTNERSHIPS AND PARTNERS § 3184. Valuation of distributions [Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3184.] 

§ 3184-1. Distributions other than in money

If profits of a partnership are distributed to a partner or participant in any medium other than money, the fair market value of the thing so distributed is income to the recipient at the time as of which such thing becomes the property of the recipient. 

Thus, distributions made in securities or other property, in which the earnings of a partnership have been invested, are income to the partners or participants to the amount of the fair market value of such property at the time of the transfer. § 3185. Sale or other disposition of partner's interest 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3185.] 

§ 3185-1. Readjustment of partnership interests (a) When a partner sells or makes other disposition of his interest in a partnership, the partner realizes a gain or loss measured by the difference between the amount realized for his interest and the sum of the adjusted cost or other basis determined under sec. 3113 (a) to him of his interest in the partnership, increased

PARTNERSHIPS AND PARTNERS 

(1) by the amount of any additional contributions made by such partner to the capital of the partnership and (2) by the amount of any undistributed profits belonging to such partner, whether or not credited to his capital account, and decreased by the amount of any profits of the partnership belonging to such partner which have not been subject to tax in the hands of such partner under this Act or a prior income tax act. (b) The amount realized from a sale or other disposition of a partner's share of the capital of a partnership is the sum of any money received plus the fair market value of any property which is received. The fair market value of property is a question of fact, but only in rare and extraordinary cases will property be considered to have no fair market value. (c) If a new partner is admitted to the partnership, or an existing partnership is reorganized, the facts as to such change or reorganization should be fully set forth in the next return of income, in order that the Secretary may determine whether any gain has been realized or loss sustained by any partner. § 3186. Distributions in liquidation 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3186.] 

§ 3186-1. Distributions in liquidation

Amounts distributed in complete liquidation of a partnership are to be treated as in full payment in exchange for the partners' shares of the capital of such partnership, and amounts distributed in partial liquidation of a partnership are to be treated as in part or full payment for the partners' shares of the capital of such partnership. The phrase "amounts distributed in partial liquidation" means one of a series of distribution in complete cancellation or redemption of all or a portion of the capital of such partnership. 

The gain or loss to a partner from a distribution in liquidation is to be determined, as provided in sec. 3185 (a) and sec. 3185–1, by comparing the amount of the distribution with the cost or other basis of his interest in the partnership; but the gain or loss will be recognized only to the extent provided in sec. 3185 (b).

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3201.] 

§ 3201-1. Tax on life insurance companies (a) All life insurance companies, as defined in sec. 3201(a) (including a foreign life insurance company carrying on a life insurance business within Puerto Rico if with respect to its Puerto Rico business it would qualify as a life insurance company under sec. 3201(a)) are subject to both normal tax and surtax. The normal tax is imposed on the normal-tax net income (as defined in sec. 3201 (c)) and the surtax is imposed on the surtax net income (as defined in sec. 3201 (d)) at the rates provided in sec. 3013 (b) and in sec. 3015 (b). Such companies are also subject to an additional tax as provided by sec. 3406. (b) The net income of life insurance companies differs from the net income of other corporations. See sec. 3203. Life insurance companies are entitled, in computing normal-tax net income and surtax net income, to the credits provided in sec. 3026 in the manner and to the extent provided in secs. 3013 (a) and 3015 (a), respectively. (c) All provisions of the statute and of these regulations not inconsistent with the specific provisions of secs. 3201 to 3203, inclusive, are applicable to the assessment and collection of the tax imposed by sec. 3201 (b), and life insurance companies are subject to the same penalties as are provided in the case of returns and payment of income tax by other corporations. 

In determining whether an insurance company is a "life insurance company" as defined in sec. 3201, no reserve shall be

Gross income of life insurance companies 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3202.] 

§ 3202-1. Gross income of life insurance companies 

Gross income in the case of life insurance companies means the gross amount of income received from interest, dividends, and rents, any profits realized from the sale of the property of the company, and all gains, benefits and income reported to Commonwealth, State or Territorial insurance departments. 

§ 3202-2. Life insurance reserves 

(a) The term "reserves required by law" is defined in sec. 

3202 (b). In the case of an assessment life insurance company or association, life insurance reserves include sums actually deposited by such company or association with the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, State, or Territorial officers pursuant to law as guaranty or reserve funds, and any funds maintained under the charter or articles of incorporation or association of such company or association, exclusively for the payment of claims arising under certificates of membership or policies issued upon the assessment plan and not subject to any other use. (b) Life insurance reserves, must be required by law either by express statutory provisions or by rules and regulations of the insurance department of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, a State, Territory, or the District of Columbia when promulgated in the exercise of a power conferred by statute, but such requirement, without more, is not conclusive; for example life insurance reserves do not include reserves required to be maintained to provide for ordinary running expenses of a business definite in amount, and which must be currently paid by every company from its income if its business is to continue, such as taxes, salaries and unpaid brokerage; nor do they include the net value of risks reinsured in

T.S 3202-2 

Ch. 253

other solvent companies; liability for premiums paid in advance; liability for annual and deferred dividends declared or apportioned; liability for dividends left on deposit at interest; liability for accrued but unsettled policy claims whether known or unreported; liability for supplementary contracts not involving, at the time with respect to which the liability is computed, life, health or accident contingencies. (c) In any case where reserves are claimed, sufficient information must be filed with the return to enable the Secretary to determine the validity of the claim. Only reserves which are required by law or insurance department ruling, which are peculiar to insurance companies, and which are dependent upon interest earnings for their maintenance will be considered as life insurance reserves. (d) In the case of life insurance companies issuing policies covering life, health, and accident insurance combined in one policy issued on the weekly premium payment plan, continuing for life and not subject to cancellation, it is required that reserve funds thereon be based upon recognized mortality or morbidity tables covering disability benefits of the kind contained in policies issued by this particular class of companies but they need not be required by law. § 3203. Net income of life insurance companies 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3203.] § 3203-1. Net income and deductions 

(a) In general. The net income of a life insurance company is its gross amount of income received during the taxable year from interest, dividends, rents, any profits realized from the sale of its property, and all gains, benefits and income reported to the corresponding governmental authority, less the deductions provided in sec. 3023 for tax-exempt interest, the excess, if any, of the reserve deduction specified in sec. 3203 (a) (2) over the amount of such interest, the deduction for deferred dividends provided in sec. 3023 (a) (3), investment expenses, real estate expenses, depreciation, and interest paid. In addition to the limitations on deductions relating to real estate owned and occupied by a life insurance company provided in sec. 3203 (b), and the limitation on the deduction for investment expenses where general expenses are allocated to investment income provided in sec. 3203 (a)(4), life 10

Supp. G

INSURANCE COMPANIES 

T.13 § 3203-1 insurance companies are subject to the limitation on deductions provided in sec. 3024(a) (5). Life insurance companies are entitled to the net operating loss deduction provided in sec. 3023 (s), see secs. 3205 and 3205–1, and as to the credit with respect to taxes of foreign countries, the United States and possessions of the United States to the extent provided in sec. 3131, see sec. 3206. (b) Tax-exempt interest. Interest which in the case of other taxpayers is excluded from gross income by sec. 3022 (b) (4) but included in the gross income of a life insurance company by sec. 

3202 is allowed as a deduction from gross income by sec. 3203 (a) (1). (c) Investment expenses. (1) As used in the Act, the term "general expenses" means any expense incurred for the benefit of more than one department of the company rather than for the benefit of a particular department thereof. Any assignment of such expense to the investment department of the company for which a deduction is claimed under sec. 3203 (a) (4) subjects the entire deduction for investment expenses to the limitation provided in that section. The accounting procedure employed is not conclusive as to whether any assignment has in fact been made. Investment expenses do not include Commonwealth income taxes. (2) If no general expenses are assigned to or included in investment expenses the deduction may consist of investment expenses actually paid during the taxable year in which case an itemized schedule of such expenses must be appended to the return. (3) Invested assets for the purpose of sec. 3203 (a) (4) and this section are those which are owned and used, and to the extent used, for the purpose of producing the income specified in sec. 3202. 

They do not include real estate owned and occupied, and to the extent owned and occupied, by the company. If general expenses are assigned to or included in investment expenses, the maximum allowance will not be granted unless it is shown to the satisfaction of the Secretary that such allowance is justified by a reasonable assignment of actual expenses. (d) Taxes and expenses with respect to real estate. The deduction for taxes and expenses under sec. 3203 (a) (5) includes taxes and expenses paid during the taxable year exclusively upon or with respect to real estate owned by the company and any sum representing taxes imposed upon a shareholder of the company upon his interest as shareholder which is paid by the company without reimbursement from the shareholder. No deduction shall be 11

T.§ 3203-1 

Ch. 253

allowed, however, for taxes, expenses, and depreciation upon or with respect to any real estate owned by the company except to the extent used for the purpose of producing investment income. 

See paragraph (c) of this section. As to real estate owned and occupied by the company, see sec. 3203–2. (e) Depreciation. The deduction allowed for depreciation is, except as provided in sec. 3203 (b), identical with that allowed other corporations by sec. 3023 (1). The amount allowed by sec. 3023 (1) in the case of life insurance companies is limited to depreciation sustained on the property used, and to the extent used, for the purpose of producing the income specified in sec. 3202. (f) Interest paid. Interest paid consists of interest paid on indebtedness (except indebtedness incurred or continued to purchase or carry tax-exempt securities as set forth in sec. 3203 (a) (7)). Interest on indebtedness includes interest on dividends held on deposit and surrendered during the taxable year. Life insurance reserves as defined in sec. 3202–2 are not indebtedness. Dividends left with the company to accumulate at interest are a debt and not a reserve liability. Amounts in the nature of interest include so-called excess-interest dividends as well as guaranteed interest paid within the taxable year on insurance or annuity contracts (or contracts arising out of insurance or annuity contracts) which do not involve at the time of payment, life, health, or accident contingencies. It is immaterial whether the optional mode of settlement specified in the insurance or annuity contract arises from an option exercised by the insured during his or her lifetime or from an option exercised by a beneficiary after the policy has matured, frequently referred to as a supplementary contract not involving life contingencies; for example, a contract to pay the insurance benefit in 10 annual installments. No distinction is made based on the person choosing the method of payment and the full amount of the interest paid and not merely the guaranteed interest, is considered as interest paid. § 3203-2. Real estate owned and occupied. 

No deduction shall be made for any taxes, expenses, or depreciation on account of any real estate owned and occupied in whole or in part by a life insurance company unless there is included in the return of gross income the rental value of the space so occupied. 

Such rental value shall not be less than a sum which in addition to any rents received from other tenants shall provide a net income 12

Supp. G

T.13 § 3204-1 

INSURANCE COMPANIES 

(after deducting taxes, depreciation, and other expenses) at the rate of 4 percent per annum of the book value at the end of the taxable year of the real estate so owned and occupied. For example, if the book value of a parcel of real estate owned and occupied in whole or in part by the company is $1,000,000, the rents received from other tenants $30,000, taxes and expenses $40,000, and depreciation $20,000, the company would have to include in its gross income a sum not less than $70,000 ($40,000 taxes and expenses, plus $20,000 depreciation, minus $30,000 rents from tenants, plus 4 percent of $1,000,000) as the rental value of the space occupied by it in order to avail itself of the deductions of $40,000 and $20,000. In any case the rents received from other tenants must be included in gross income. § 3203-3. Foreign life insurance companies 

Foreign life insurance companies holding reserve funds upon business transacted within Puerto Rico are taxed under sec. 

3201(b)(2) upon their net income from sources within Puerto Rico, computed as provided in sec. 3203 (c). A foreign life insurance company not doing an insurance business within Puerto Rico and holding no reserve funds upon business transacted within Puerto Rico, but which derives income from sources within Puerto Rico as defined in sec. 3119 is subject to the tax imposed by sec. 3231 upon income derived from sources within Puerto Rico. § 3204. Insurance companies other than life or mutual 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3204.] 

§ 3204-1. Tax on insurance companies other than life or mutual (a) All insurance companies, other than life or mutual companies, are subject to the tax imposed by sec. 3204. As used in this section and secs. 3204-2 and 3204-3, the term "insurance companies" means only those companies subject to the tax imposed by sec. 3204. The net income of insurance companies is defined in sec. 3204 and differs from the net income of other corporations. All provisions of the Act and of these regulations not inconsistent with the specific provisions of sec. 3204 are applicable to the assessment and collection of the tax imposed by sec. 3204 (a), and insurance companies are subject to the same penalties as are provided in the case of returns and payment of income tax by other corporations. Since sec. 3204 provides that the underwriting and investment exhibit of the annual statement 13

T.§ 3204-1 

Ch. 253

approved by the National Convention of Insurance Commissioners shall be the basis for computing gross income and since the annual statement is rendered on the calendar year basis, the returns under sec. 3204 shall be made on the basis of the calendar year and shall be on Form 480.20. Insurance companies are entitled, in computing normal-tax net income, and surtax net income, to the credits provided in sec. 3026 in the manner and to the extent provided in secs. 

3013 (a) and 3015 (a). (b) Foreign insurance companies not carrying on an insurance business within Puerto Rico are not taxable under sec. 3204 but are taxable as other foreign corporations. See sec. 3231. (c) Insurance companies are subject to normal tax, surtax and an additional tax. The normal tax shall be computed as provided in sec. 3013 (b). For what constitutes normal-tax net income, see sec. 3013-1. The surtax shall be computed as provided in sec. 

3015 (b). For what constitutes corporation surtax net income, see sec. 3015-1. See sec. 3046 for the additional tax. For alternative tax where the net long-term capital gain for any taxable year exceeds the net short-term capital loss, see sec. 3117 (c) and the regulations thereunder. § 3204-2. Gross income of insurance companies other than life or mutual (a) Gross income as defined in sec. 3204 (b) means the gross amount of income earned during the taxable year from interest, dividends, rents, and premium income, computed on the basis of the underwriting and investment exhibit of the annual statement approved by the National Convention of Insurance Commissioners, as well as the gain derived from the sale or other disposition of property. It does not include increase in liabilities during the year on account of reinsurance treaties, remittances from the home office of a foreign insurance company to the Puerto Rico branch, borrowed money, or gross increase due to adjustments in book value of capital assets. The underwriting and investment exhibit is presumed clearly to reflect the true net income of the company, and insofar as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Income Tax Act of 1954 will be recognized and used as a basis for that purpose. All items of the exhibit, however, do not reflect an insurance company's income as defined in the Act. By reason of the definition of investment income, miscellaneous items which are intended to reflect surplus but do not properly enter into the 14

Supp. G

T.13 S 3204-2 

INSURANCE COMPANIES 

computation of income, such as dividends declared to shareholders in their capacity as such, home office remittances and receipts, and special deposits, are ignored. Gain or loss from agency balances and bills receivable not admitted as assets on the underwriting and investment exhibit will be ignored, excepting only such agency balances and bills receivable as have been allowed as deductions for worthless debts or, having been previously so allowed, are recovered during the taxable year. In computing "losses incurred" the determination of unpaid losses at the close of each year must represent actual unpaid losses as nearly as it is possible to ascertain them. (b) Every insurance company to which this section applies must be prepared to establish to the satisfaction of the Secretary that the part of the deduction for "losses incurred" which represents unpaid losses at the close of the taxable year comprises only actual unpaid losses stated in amounts which, based upon the facts in each case and the company's experience with similar cases, can be said to represent a fair and reasonable estimate of the amount the company will be required to pay. Amounts included in, or added to, the estimates of such losses which, in the opinion of the Secretary, are in excess of the actual liability determined as provided in the preceding sentence will be disallowed as a deduction. The Secretary may require any such insurance company to submit such detailed information with respect to its actual experience as is deemed necessary to establish the reasonableness of the deduction for "losses incurred". (c) That part of the deduction for "losses incurred" which represents an adjustment to "losses paid" for "salvage and reinsurance recoverable" shall, except as hereinafter provided, include all salvage in course of liquidation, and all reinsurance in process of collection not otherwise taken into account as a reduction of "losses paid", outstanding at the end of the taxable year. 

Salvage in course of liquidation includes all property (other than cash), real or personal, tangible or intangible, except that which may not be included by reason of express statutory provisions, or rules and regulations of the Superintendent of Insurance, of the 

Commonwealth of Puerto Rico. Such salvage in course of liquidation shall be taken into account to the extent of the value thereof at the end of the taxable year as determined from a fair and reasonable estimate based upon either the facts in each case or the company's experience with similar cases. § 3208.

Mutual insurance companies other than life 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3208.] 

§ 3208-1. Gross income of mutual insurance companies other than life (a) The gross income of mutual insurance companies (other than life) consists of their total revenue from the operation of the business and of their income from all other sources within the taxable year, except as otherwise provided by the Act. Gross income includes net premiums (that is, gross premiums less returned premiums on policies canceled and premiums on policies not taken), investment income, profits from the sale of assets, and all gains, profits, and income reported to Commonwealth or State insurance departments, except income specifically exempt from tax. Premiums received by mutual marine insurance companies which are paid out for reinsurance should be eliminated from gross income and the payments for reinsurance from disbursements. Deposit premiums on perpetual risks received and returned by mutual fire insurance companies should be treated in the same manner, as no reserve will be recognized covering liability for such deposits. The earnings on such deposits, including such portion, if any, of the deposits as is not returned to the policyholders upon cancellation of the policies, must be included in the gross income. A net decrease in reserve funds required by law within the taxable year must be included in the gross income to the extent that such funds are released to the general uses of the company and increase its free assets. Any net decrease in reserves shall be added to the gross income, unless the company shall show that such decrease resulted from the application of reserves to the purpose for which they were established. (b) All provisions of the Act and of these regulations not inconsistent with the specific provisions of sec. 3208 are applicable to the assessment and collection of the tax imposed upon mutual insurance companies other than life, and such companies are subject to the same penalties as are provided in the case of returns and payment of income tax by other corporations. The return shall be on Form 480.20. § 3208-2. Deductions allowed mutual insurance companies other than life insurance companies Mutual insurance companies (other than life insurance com- 17

Reserve funds "required by law" include not only reserves required by express statutory provisions but also reserves required by the rules and the regulations of the Commonwealth, State or Territorial insurance departments when promulgated in the exercise of an appropriate power conferred by statute, but do not include assets required to be held for the ordinary running expenses of the business, such as taxes, salaries, reinsurance, and unpaid brokerage. Only reserves commonly recognized as reserve funds in insurance accounting are to be taken into consideration in computing the net addition to reserve funds required by law. In the case of a fire insurance company the only reserve fund commonly recognized is the “unearned-premium" fund. § 3208-4. Special deductions allowed mutual marine insurance companies

Mutual marine insurance companies should include in gross income the gross premiums collected and received by them less amounts paid for reinsurance. (See secs. 3208(b) and 3208–1.)

They may deduct from gross income amounts repaid to policyholders on account of premiums previously paid by them, together with the interest actually paid upon such amounts between the date of ascertainment and the date of payment thereof. The remainder of the premiums accordingly forms part of the net income of the company, except to the extent that it is subject to the deductions allowed such insurance companies and other corporations. § 3208-5. Special deductions allowed mutual insurance companies 

Mutual insurance companies (including interinsurers and reciprocal underwriters, but not including mutual life and mutual marine insurance companies), which require their members to make premium deposits to provide for losses and expenses, are allowed to deduct from gross income the aggregate amount of premium deposits returned to their policyholders or retained for the payment of losses, expenses, and reinsurance reserves. In determining the amount of premium deposits retained by a mutual fire or mutual casualty insurance company for the payment of losses, expenses, and reinsurance reserves, it will be presumed that losses and expenses have been paid out of earnings and profits other than premiums to the extent of such earnings and profits. 

If, however, any portion of such amount is applied during the taxable year to the payment of losses, expenses, or reinsurance reserves, for which a separate allowance is taken, then such portion is not deductible; and if any portion of such amount for which an allowance is taken is subsequently applied to the payment of expenses, losses, or reinsurance reserves, then such payment can not be separately deducted. The amount of premium deposits retained for the payment of expenses and losses, and the amount 19

T.§ 3208-5 

Ch. 253

of such expenses and losses, may not both be deducted. A company which invests part of the premium deposits so retained by it in interest-bearing securities may nevertheless deduct such part, but not the interest received on such securities. A mutual fire insurance company which has a guaranty capital is taxed like other mutual fire insurance companies. A stock fire insurance company, operated on the mutual plan to the extent of paying dividends to certain classes of policyholders, may make a return on the same basis as a mutual fire insurance company with respect to its business conducted on the mutual plan.

Payment of tax 3218-1. Date on which tax shall be paid by nonresident alien individual § 3211. Tax on nonresident alien individuals 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3211.] § 3211-1. Taxation of aliens in general 

For the purposes of the Income Tax Act, alien individuals are divided generally into two classes, namely, resident aliens and nonresident aliens. Resident aliens are, in general, taxable the same as other residents of Puerto Rico, that is, a resident alien is taxable on income derived from all sources including sources without Puerto Rico. Nonresident aliens are taxable only on income from sources within Puerto Rico. For classification of nonresident aliens, see sec. 3211-7.

20

Supp. H

T.13 § 3211-3 

 § 3211-2. Definition 

(a) A "nonresident alien individual" means an individual (1) Who is not a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico; and (2) Who is not a citizen of the United States. The term includes a nonresident fiduciary. 

(b) An alien actually present in Puerto Rico who is not a mere transient or sojourner is a resident of Puerto Rico for purposes of the income tax. Whether he is a transient is determined by his intentions with regard to the length and nature of his stay. A mere floating intention, indefinite as to time, to return to another country is not sufficient to constitute him a transient. If he lives in Puerto Rico and has no definite intention as to his stay, he is a resident. One who comes to Puerto Rico for a definite purpose which in its nature may be promptly accomplished is a transient; but if his purpose is of such a nature that an extended stay may be necessary for its accomplishment, and to that end the alien makes his home temporarily in Puerto Rico, he becomes a resident, though it may be his intention at all times to return to his domicile abroad when the purpose for which he came has been consummated or abandoned. An alien whose stay in Puerto Rico is limited to a definite period by the immigration laws is not a resident of Puerto Rico within the meaning of this section, in the absence of exceptional circumstances. § 3211-3. Alien seamen as residents

In order to determine whether an alien seaman is a resident within the meaning of the Income Tax Act, it is necessary to decide whether the presumption of nonresidence is overcome by facts showing that he has established a residence in Puerto Rico (as used in sec. 1 of the Federal Relations Act) which includes not only the Island of Puerto Rico, but the other islands adjacent thereto (La Mona, Vieques, Culebra, Cayo de Berberia, Cardona, Caja de Muerto) and excludes other places. Residence may be established on a vessel regularly engaged in coastwise trade, but the mere fact that a sailor makes his home on a vessel flying the United States flag and engaged in foreign trade is not sufficient to establish residence in Puerto Rico, even though the vessel, while carrying on foreign trade, touches at Puerto Rican ports. An alien seaman may acquire an actual residence in Puerto Rico within the rules laid down in sec. 3211-4, although the nature of his calling requires him to be absent for a long period from the place where 21

T.§ 3211-3 

Ch. 253

his residence is established. An alien seaman may acquire such a residence at a sailors' boarding house or hotel, but such a claim should be carefully scrutinized in order to make sure that such residence is bona fide. The taking out of first citizenship papers in 

Puerto Rico is proof of residence in Puerto Rico from the time the papers are taken out, unless rebutted by other evidence showing an intention to be a transient.

Codification. Sec. 2 of the Organic Act of Puerto Rico, approved by Congress March 2, 1917" was changed to "sec. 

1 of the Federal Relations Act". 

§ 3211-4. Proof of residence of alien 

(a) The following rules of evidence shall govern in determining whether or not an alien within Puerto Rico has acquired residence therein within the meaning of the Income Tax Act. An alien, by reason of his alienage, is presumed to be a nonresident alien. Such presumption may be overcome (1) In the case of an alien who presents himself for determination of tax liability before departure for his native country by (i) proof that the alien, at least six months before the date he so presents himself, has filed in Puerto Rico a declaration of his intention to become a citizen of the United States under the naturalization laws, or (ii) proof of acts and statements of the alien showing a definite intention to acquire residence in Puerto Rico or showing that his stay in Puerto Rico has been of such an extended nature as to constitute him a resident; (2) In other cases by (i) proof that the alien has filed a declaration of his intention to become a citizen of the United States under the naturalization laws, or (ii) proof of acts and statements of an alien showing a definite intention to acquire residence in Puerto Rico or showing that his stay in Puerto Rico has been of such an extended nature to constitute him a resident. (b) In any case in which an alien seeks to overcome the presumption of nonresidence under paragraph (a) (1) (i) or (2) (ii) of this section, if the officer or employee of the Bureau of Income Tax who examines the alien is in doubt as to the facts, such officer or employee may, to assist him in determining the facts, require an affidavit or affidavits setting forth the facts relied upon, executed by some creditable person or persons, other than the alien and members of his family who have known the alien at least six months before the date of execution of the affidavit or affidavits. 22

Supp. H T.13 3211-7 

 § 3211-5. Loss of residence by alien 

An alien who has acquired residence in Puerto Rico retains his status as a resident until he abandons the same and actually departs from Puerto Rico. An intention to change his residence does not change his status as a resident alien to that of a nonresident alien. Thus, an alien who has acquired a residence in 

Puerto Rico is taxable as a resident for the remainder of his stay in Puerto Rico. § 3211-6. Duty of employer to determine status of alien employee 

If wages are paid to aliens without withholding the tax, the employer should be prepared to prove the status of the alien as provided in secs. 3211-1 to 3211-5, inclusive. An employer may rely upon the evidence of residence afforded by the fact than an alien has taken out first citizenship papers, or an equivalent certificate of the alien establishing residence. An employer who seeks to account for failure to withhold in the past, is permitted to prove the former status of the alien by any competent evidence. The written statement of the alien employee may ordinarily be relied upon by the employer as proof that the alien is a resident of 

Puerto Rico. 

§ 3211-7. Taxation of nonresident alien individuals (a) In general. For the purposes of this section and secs. 3212-1, 3213-1, 3214-1, 3215-1, and 3217-2, nonresident alien individuals are divided into three classes: (1) Nonresident alien individuals not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year and deriving in such taxable year an amount of not more than $22,200 in the aggregate which is the gross amount of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income from sources within Puerto Rico plus the excess of capital gains over capital losses, determined in accordance with paragraph (b) (2) of this section, from sources within Puerto Rico; (2) nonresident alien individuals not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year and deriving in such taxable year an amount of more than $22,000 in the aggregate which is the gross amount of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income from sources within Puerto Rico plus the excess of capital gains over capital losses, determined in accordance with paragraph (b) (2) of this section, from sources within Puerto Rico; 23

 § 3212. Gross income [Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3212.] 

§ 3212-1. Gross income of nonresident alien individuals (a) In general. (1) In general, in the case of nonresident alien individuals "gross income" means only the gross income from sources within Puerto Rico. See sec. 3119 and the regulations thereunder. The items of gross income from sources without Puerto Rico and therefore not taxable to nonresident aliens are described in sec. 3119 (c). As to who are nonresident alien individuals, see secs. 3211-2 to 3211-6, inclusive. (2) Income received by a resident alien from sources without Puerto Rico is taxable although such person may become a nonresident alien subsequent to its receipt and before the close of the taxable year. Conversely, income received by a nonresident alien from sources without Puerto Rico is not taxable though such person may become a resident alien subsequent to its receipt and before the close of the taxable year. (b) No Puerto Rico business. The gross income of a nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year, whether such alien comes within sec. 3211(a) or sec. 3211 (c), is gross income from sources within Puerto Rico consisting of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income and any gain from the sale or exchange of a capital asset to the extent required to be included in gross income under the provisions of sec. 3211 (a) (1) (B) or sec. 3211(c). (c) Puerto Rico business. The gross income of a nonresident alien individual who at any time within the taxable year was engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico is not limited to the items of gross income specified in sec. 3211(a), but includes any item of gross income which is treated as income from sources within Puerto Rico, except those items which are exempt from taxation by statute or which are not taxable by the Commonwealth under the Constitution of the United States. See secs. 3022(b), 3112, 3116, 3119, and 3212. (d) What constitutes engaging in trade or business within 

Puerto Rico. (1) In general, any nonresident alien individual who performs personal services within Puerto Rico is considered as being engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico and, therefore, his net income from sources within Puerto Rico, including his com- 27

T.§ 3212-1 

Ch. 253

pensation, is subject to the normal tax and the surtax. However, the phrase "engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico" does not apply to the personal services performed within Puerto Rico for a nonresident alien individual, foreign partnership, or foreign corporation, not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico, by a nonresident alien individual temporarily present in Puerto Rico for a period or periods not exceeding a total of 90 days during the taxable year and whose compensation for such services does not exceed in the aggregate $3,000. Such compensation is not income from sources within Puerto Rico. See sec. 3119 (a) (3). As to the exclusion from gross income of the official compensation received by employees of foreign governments or of international organizations, see sec. 3116 (h). (2) The effecting of transactions in Puerto Rico in stocks, securities, or commodities (including hedging transactions) through a resident broker, commission agent, or custodian does not bring a nonresident alien individual within the class of nonresident alien individuals engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico, but if a nonresident alien individual by reason of rendering personal services in Puerto Rico, or for other reasons, is classed as a nonresident alien individual engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico, he is taxable upon all income from sources within Puerto Rico, including profits derived from the effecting of such transactions. Such a nonresident alien individual is required to include in gross income capital gains, gains from hedging transactions, and profits derived from the sale within Puerto Rico of personal property, or of real property located therein. The term "commodities" means only goods of a kind customarily dealt in on an organized commodity exchange, and does not include merchandise in the ordinary channels of commerce.

Sec. 3214 specifically provides that a nonresident alien individual shall not be allowed the credits against net income for personal exemption and dependents under sec. 3025. 

§ 3215. Allowance of deductions [Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3215.] 

§ 3215-1. Allowance of deductions to nonresident alien individuals (a) No Puerto Rico business. (1) General rule. In general, a nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year is not entitled to any allowance of deductions (except as provided in paragraph (b) (2) of sec. 3211-7 or credits even though he may file a return of income. (2) Aggregate more than $22,200. Unless a nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year and having, for such year from sources within Puerto Rico, income described in sec. 3211(a)(1) in a gross amount of more than $22,200 shall file or cause to filed CCC 30

Supp. H

T.13 § 3215-1 with the Secretary a true and accurate return of his total income described in sec. 3211(a) (1) from sources within Puerto Rico as required by paragraph (a) (2) of sec. 3217-2, the tax shall be collected on the basis of gross amount of such income described in sec. 3211(a) (1). Where such nonresident alien has various sources of income described in sec. 3211(a) (1) from within Puerto 

Rico, as, for instance, from an estate or trust, from stocks or bonds held directly by him, or from securities held for him by a custodian resident in Puerto Rico, so that his income described in sec. 

3211 (a) (1) from Puerto Rico sources is in excess of $22,200 and a return of income is not filed by him or on his behalf, the Secretary will cause a return of income to be made and include therein the income described in sec. 3211(a)(1) from all sources within Puerto 

Rico concerning which he has information without allowance for deductions and credits, and will assess the tax and collect it from one or more of the sources of income within Puerto Rico. Such nonresident alien shall make or have made a full and accurate return on Form 480.0 of all income described in sec. 3211(a) (1) from sources within Puerto Rico. Such returns shall contain or be verified by a written declaration that it is made under the penalties of perjury. As to the duty of the representative or agent of such alien to file the return and pay the tax, see paragraph (b) (2) of sec. 3217-2, which is hereby made equally applicable in the case of a nonresident alien individual coming within the provisions of this subparagraph. (b) Puerto Rico business. Unless a nonresident alien individual who at any time within the taxable year was engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico shall file, or cause to be filed, with the Secretary, a true and accurate return of his total income from sources within Puerto Rico, as required by paragraph (b)(1) of sec. 3217-2, the tax shall be collected on the basis of the gross income (not the net income) from sources within Puerto Rico. 

Where such a nonresident alien has various sources of income within Puerto Rico, and a return of income was not filed by him or on his behalf, the Secretary will cause a return of income to be made and include therein the income of such nonresident alien from all sources concerning which he has information, without allowance for deductions or credits, and will assess the tax and collect it from one or more of the sources of income of such nonresident alien within Puerto Rico. 31

§ 3217. Returns 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3217.] 

§ 3217-1.

Time and place for filing returns of nonresident alien individuals (a) In the case of a nonresident alien individual who for the taxable year does not have wages subject to withholding at the source under sec. 3141, the return must be made on or before the fifteenth day of the sixth full calendar month following the close of the taxable year. In the case of any return for a fractional part of a year, the Secretary may, upon a showing by the taxpayer of unusual circumstances, prescribe a later time for the filing of the return. The return must be filed with the Secretary in care of the 

Bureau of Income Tax. For failure to make and file return within the time prescribed, see sec. 3291. For cases in which no return is required, see paragraph (a) of sec. 3217-2. (b) In the case of nonresident alien individuals who have wages subject to withholding under sec. 3141, the general rule provided in paragraph (a) of this section with respect to the filing of the return has no application. Such aliens are required to file their returns and to pay the tax at the time prescribed generally for Puerto Rico residents. As to the time of filing the return in the case of Puerto Rico residents, see secs. 3053 and 3053–1. 

§ 3217-2. Return of income 

(a) No Puerto Rico business. (1) General rule. If the tax liability of a nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year is fully satisfied at the source, a return of income is not required. 

A nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year shall make or have made a return on Form 480.0 with respect to that portion of his income received from sources within Puerto Rico upon which the tax was not fully satisfied at the source, including dividends or profits received from a foreign corporation or partnership which are treated as income from sources within Puerto Rico under sec. 

3119 (a) (2) (B), and shall pay the balance of the tax shown to be due. (2) Aggregate more than $22,200. A nonresident alien individual not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time during the taxable year, and deriving in such year more 32

Supp. H 

T.13 § 3218 than $22,200 gross amount of income described in sec. 3211(a) (1) from sources within Puerto Rico, shall make or have made a full and accurate return on Form 480.0 of all his income described in sec. 3211(a) (1) from sources within Puerto Rico, including gains from transactions described in sec. 3211 (a) (1) (B). As to the duty of the representative or agent of such alien to file the return and pay the tax, see paragraph (b) (2) of this section, which is hereby made equally applicable in the case of a nonresident alien coming within the provisions of this subparagraph. (b) Puerto Rico business. (1) If a nonresident alien individual at any time within the taxable year is engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico, he shall make or have made a full and accurate return on Form 480.0 of his income received from all sources within 

Puerto Rico. 

(2) The responsible representative or agent within Puerto Rico or a nonresident alien individual who at any time within the taxable year was engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico shall make in behalf of his nonresident alien principal, a return of, and shall pay the tax on, all income from sources within Puerto Rico coming within his control as representative or agent. The agency appointment will determine how completely the agent is substituted for the principal for tax purposes. See sec. 3051-2. Any person who collects interest or dividends on deposited securities of such a nonresident alien, and sells such securities under special instructions shall not be deemed merely by reason of such acts to be the responsible representative or agent of the nonresident alien. (c) Refund based on return. Where upon filing a return of income it appears that such a nonresident alien is not liable for tax, but nevertheless a tax shall have been withheld at the source, there should, in order to obtain a refund on the basis of the showing made by the return, be attached to it a statement showing accurately the amounts of tax withheld, with the names and postoffice addresses of all withholding agents. (d) Verification of returns. A return on Form 480.0, shall contain or be verified by a written declaration that it is made under the penalties of perjury.

Tax on foreign corporations and partnerships 

[Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3231.] 

§ 3231-1. Taxation of foreign corporations and partnerships (a) General. For the purposes of this section and secs. 3231-2, 3232-1, 3235-1, 3235-2, and 3236-1, foreign corporations or partnerships are divided into two classes: (1) Foreign corporations or partnerships not engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico at any time within the taxable year, referred to in the regulations as nonresident foreign corporations or partnerships (see sec. 3411-8); and (2) foreign corporations or partnerships which at any time within the taxable year are engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico, referred to in the regulations as resident foreign corporations or partnerships (see sec. 3411-8). 34

Supp. I

T.13 3231-1 

(b) Nonresident foreign corporations or partnerships. (1) A nonresident foreign corporation or partnership is liable to the tax upon the amount received from sources within Puerto Rico, determined under the provisions of sec. 3119, which is fixed or determinable annual or periodical gains, profits, and income. For the purposes of sec. 3231(a), the term "amount received" means "gross income". Specific items of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income are enumerated in the Act as interest (except interest on deposits with persons carrying on the banking business and interest declared exempt under sec. 3022 (b) (4)), dividends, partnership profits, rents, salaries, wages, premiums, annuities, compensations, remunerations, emoluments, but other fixed or determinable annual or periodical gains, profits, and income are also subject to the tax, as, for instance, royalties. As to the definition of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income, see sec. 3143-2. (2) The fixed or determinable annual or periodical income from sources within Puerto Rico, including royalties, of a nonresident foreign corporation or partnership is taxable at the rate of 29 per cent. (c) Resident foreign corporations or partnerships. (1) A resident foreign corporation or partnership is not taxable upon the items of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income enumerated in sec. 3231 (a) at the rate specified in that section. A resident foreign corporation or partnership is, under sec. 3013, liable to a tax of 20 per cent of its normal-tax net income. The normal-tax net income of a resident foreign corporation or partnership is its net income from sources within Puerto Rico (gross income from sources within Puerto Rico minus the statutory deductions provided in secs. 

3023 and 3232) less the credit provided in sec. 3026 (a). (2) A resident foreign corporation or partnership is, under sec. 3015, also liable to a tax on the amount of its surtax net income in excess of $25,000. The surtax net income of a resident foreign corporation or partnership is its net income from sources within Puerto Rico (gross income from sources within Puerto Rico minus the statutory deductions provided in secs. 3023 and 3232) less the credits provided in sec. 3026 (a) and (b). See sec. 3406 for the additional tax of 5 per cent levied upon the total of the normal tax and surtax as determined under the provisions of chapters 252 and 253 of L.P.R.A., Title 13. 

1962 Vol. 1, No. 3 35

T.§ 3231-1 

Ch. 253

(d) Meaning of terms used. As used in secs. 3119, 3143, 3144, 3211 and 3231, the phrase "engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico" includes the performance of personal services within Puerto Rico at any time within the taxable year. Such phrase does not include the effecting of transactions in Puerto Rico in stocks, securities, or commodities (including hedging transactions) through a resident broker, commission agent, or custodian. The term "commodities" means only goods of a kind customarily dealt in on an organized commodity exchange and does not include merchandise in the ordinary channels of commerce. 

ANNOTATIONS 

1. Prior regulation Generally. Pursuant to our Income

Tax Act in force in 1940, foreign corporations having an office or doing business in Puerto Rico were not the only ones subject to our income tax. Foreign corporations having no office or doing no business in Puerto Rico were also subject to taxes on income received from sources within 

Puerto Rico. Porto Rico Telephone Co. v. Secretary of the Treasury, 1957, 79 P.R.R. 845. 

§ 3231-2. Gross income of foreign corporations and partnerships (a) In general. In the case of a foreign corporation or partnership including a life insurance company not carrying on an insurance business within Puerto Rico and holding no reserve funds upon business transacted within Puerto Rico, an insurance company other than life or mutual not carrying on an insurance business within Puerto Rico, and a mutual insurance company other than life not carrying on an insurance business within Puerto Rico, the term "gross income" means gross income from sources within Puerto Rico as defined and described in sec. 3119. See secs. 

3119(a)-1 to 3119 (e)-4, inclusive. The items of gross income from sources without Puerto Rico and therefore not taxable to foreign corporations or partnerships are described in sec. 3119 (c). As to the definitions of a foreign corporation or partnership, see sec. 

3411(a)(2), (3) and (5). As to foreign life insurance companies, see sec. 3203–3. As to foreign corporations or partnerships formed or availed of to avoid tax, upon shareholders or partners, see sec. 3102-4. (b) Nonresident foreign corporations and partnerships. A nonresident foreign corporation or partnership is taxable under sec. 

3231 (a) only on fixed or determinable annual or periodical gross income received from sources within Puerto Rico. 1962 Vol. 1, No. 3 36

Supp. I

T.13 § 3232-1 

(c) Resident foreign corporations and partnerships. (1) The gross income from sources within Puerto Rico of a resident foreign corporation or partnership is not limited to the items of fixed or determinable annual or periodical income referred to in sec. 3231(a), but includes every item of gross income which is treated as income from sources within Puerto Rico, except those items which are specifically exempt from taxation by statute or which are not taxable by the Commonwealth under the Constitution of the United States. See secs. 3022 (b) and 3119. (2) A resident foreign corporation or partnership is also required to include in its gross income capital gains, gains from hedging transactions, and profits derived from the sale within Puerto Rico of personal property, or of real property located therein. (3) A foreign corporation or partnership which effects transactions in Puerto Rico in stocks, securities, or commodities (including hedging transactions) through a resident broker, commission agent, or custodian is not merely by reason of such transactions considered as being engaged in trade or business within Puerto Rico which would cause it to be classed as a resident foreign corporation or partnership. However, a foreign corporation or partnership which at any time within the taxable year is otherwise engaged in trade or business in Puerto Rico, being a resident foreign corporation or partnership, is taxable upon all income derived from sources within Puerto Rico, including the profits realized from such transactions.

§ 3271. Definition of deficiency [Text of Act, see 13 L.P.R.A. § 3271.] § 3271-1. Deficiency defined 

(a) The term “deficiency” means the excess of the tax imposed by the Act over the sum of the amount shown as the tax by the taxpayer upon his return and the amounts previously assessed (or collected without assessment) as a deficiency; but such sum shall first be reduced by the amount of rebates made. If no return is made, or if the return (except a return on Form 480.0A pursuant to sec. 3051(f)) does not show any tax, for the purposes of the definition "the amount shown as the tax by the taxpayer upon his return" shall be considered as zero. Accordingly, in any such case, if no deficiencies have been assessed, or collected without assessment, and no rebates have been made, the deficiency is the amount of the tax imposed by the Act. Additional tax shown on an "amended return", so-called, filed after the due date of the return for the taxable year, is a deficiency within the meaning of the Income Tax Act. 

(b) For the purposes of the definition, the tax imposed by the Act and the tax shown on the return shall both be determined without regard to the credit provided in sec. 3025 for tax withheld 40

Supp. L

DEFICIENCIES 

T.13 § 3271-1 on wages, and without regard to the credit provided in sec. 3032 for taxes withheld at the source. Payments on account of estimated tax, like other payments of tax by the taxpayer, shall likewise be disregarded in the determination of a deficiency. (c) The computation by the Secretary, pursuant to sec. 3051(f), of the tax imposed by the Act shall be considered as having been made by the taxpayer and the tax so computed shall be considered as the tax shown by the taxpayer upon his return. (d) If so much of the credits claimed on the return for taxes withheld at the source is greater than the amount of such credits allowable, the unpaid portion of the tax attributable to such difference will be collected not as a deficiency but as an underpayment of the tax shown on the return. (e) This section may be illustrated by the following example: 

Example. The amount of tax shown by the taxpayer upon his return for the calendar year 1955 was $1,500. The taxpayer had no amounts previously assessed (or collected without assessment) as a deficiency. He claimed a credit in the amount of $2,000 for tax withheld at source on wages under sec. 3141 and a refund of $500 (not a rebate under sec. 3271) was made to him as an overpayment of tax for the taxable year. It is later determined that the correct tax for the taxable year is $1,750. A deficiency of $250 is determined as follows: $1,750

None
